Consider the vectors



$$
\mathbf{c_1}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$



If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then what is $x_1+x_2?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=5 \\ -{x}_{1} &=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $x_1=5,$ which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ 4(5)+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ {x}_{2} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 3(5)+(-15) & =0 \\ 0 & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15,$ which means

$$
5 \mathbf{c_1}-15 \mathbf{c_2} = \mathbf{d}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2=5-15=-10.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{array} \right]
$$



Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{array} \right]
$$



Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_3=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.
$$

So the solution of the system is $x_1=-3, x_2=-1, x_3=2,$ which means

$$
-3 \mathbf{a_1}- \mathbf{a_2} +2 \mathbf{a_3}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3=-3-1+2=-2.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=4 \\ x+2y &=16\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x+2y &=16 \\
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\\
	4+3y &=16\\
	3y &=12\\
	y &=4
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x &= 4 + y \\
	   &= 4 + (4) \\
	   &=8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2u+9v-6 &=0 \\ 2u+6v-8 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:


$$
\qquad\:\:\: \left\{\begin{aligned}{\color{red}2u+9v-6} &{\color{red}{}=0} && {\color{red}(1)} \\ {\color{blue}2u+6v-8} &{\color{blue}{}=0} && {\color{blue}(2)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$



We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \\
2u+6v &= 8 \\
2u &= 8 - 6v \\
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \\
u &= 4 - 3v
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \\
2+3v &= 0 \\
3v &= -2 \\
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \\
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \\
	2u-12 &= 0 \\
	2u &= 12 \\
	u &= 6
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$
